Clocks are set back one hour on **different days** in the US and the EU this autumn (2026):

- **US:** Sunday, **November 1, 2026** — at 2:00 a.m. local time, clocks go back to 1:00 a.m. (Daylight Saving ends on the first Sunday of November).
- **EU:** Sunday, **October 25, 2026** — at 03:00 UTC, clocks go back to 02:00 (Daylight Saving ends on the last Sunday of October).

So no, it is **not** the same day — they differ by exactly one week in 2026.

Why the two dates: each region uses a *relative* rule (first Sunday of November vs. last Sunday of October), and in most years the last Sunday of October falls immediately before the first Sunday of November. The gap is always either 7 days or about a month, depending on where the month boundaries land.

No, they're not the same day.

**US:** Clocks go back on the **first Sunday of November**. For autumn 2026 that's **November 1, 2026**, at 2 a.m. local time (11 p.m. on Saturday Oct 31 in Pacific time).

**EU:** Clocks go back on the **last Sunday of October**. For autumn 2026 that's **October 25, 2026**, at 3 a.m. local time (2 a.m. in places on Central European Time... correction: the switchover is 1 a.m. UTC = 3 a.m. CEST / 2 a.m. CET).

So in 2026 the EU switches **six days earlier** (Oct 25) than the US (Nov 1).

| Region | 2026 date | Local switch time | UTC |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU (CEST→CET) | Sun, Oct 25 | 2:00 a.m. UTC | 02:00 |
| US (e.g. Eastern EDT→EST) | Sun, Nov 1 | 1:00 a.m. UTC | 01:00 |

**Rules (which determine the dates above):**
- **US:** first Sunday in November, since the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (previously the last Sunday in October, so it *was* often the same day as the EU before 2007).
- **EU (and most of Europe):** last Sunday in October, per the EU seasonal-time rules (applies to all EU member states, plus EEA countries like Norway/Switzerland).

**A few caveats:**
- The EU time rule technically still stands; several countries (e.g. Spain, France) have kept permanent summer time under their own national laws, but the *official* EU-wide rule of switching on the last Sunday in October is what's referenced as "the EU date."
- **UK (not EU but often grouped with it):** last Sunday in October, same day as the EU — so Oct 25, 2026, too.
- **Canada:** first Sunday in November, same as the US.
- Not every US state observes DST (Hawaii, Arizona, most of Alaska; some small areas opt out).

**Bottom line:** in autumn the EU/UK switch **the last Sunday of October** and the US **the first Sunday of November**, so they are *not* the same day — in 2026 the EU/UK switch on **Oct 25** and the US on **Nov 1**.

This year (2025) they fall on the same calendar day, but the US clock change starts earlier in the day because of the time difference.

- US: Sunday, November 2, 2025 at 2:00 a.m. local time.
- EU: Sunday, November 2, 2025 at 3:00 a.m. UTC (2:00 a.m. in UTC+1 zones, e.g. Central European Time).

So yes, the same calendar day (November 2), but not the same instant: the US switch-over happens about 5–6 hours after the EU one, when viewed in UTC.

Rule behind it: the US ends daylight saving on the first Sunday in November; the EU ends it on the last Sunday of October. In 2025 those happen to be the same date.
